warmup.q: A Semaphore is a counter of permits: acquire() takes one, and release() gives one back. One starts with 5 permits. A thread calls release() without ever calling acquire(). What does availablePermits() return now?
options: 5, because the stray release is ignored
warmup.why: Permits belong to nobody. A semaphore is a counter, and release() adds one, whoever calls it. That's handy, since one thread can take a permit and another can give it back. It's also how a bug quietly raises a limit of 5 to 6, then 7. A lock would throw here; a semaphore can't, because it doesn't know who took what. The third section runs exactly this.

opening:
Picture a small shop that opens at nine. Before the doors open, its program loads three lists: the price list, the stock counts and today's offers. Three threads load them side by side. (A thread is one path of work that runs side by side with others in the same program.) The thread that opens the doors has to wait until all three are done.

One morning the doors open early, and the first customer buys a loaf of bread for 0.00. The price list was still loading.

The fix most people reach for first is a nap, Thread.sleep(2000), which feels like plenty of time. It makes every morning two seconds slower, and on the day the price list takes three seconds, bread is free again.

In Concurrent collections, a queue carried work from one thread to another. Here nothing changes hands: the threads just have to wait for each other, the way runners wait for the starting gun. In this lesson, we'll meet four tools for four shapes of waiting: a latch, a barrier, a semaphore and a phaser. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a shop that opened its doors before the prices had loaded. A latch let it open the moment the last list arrived. A barrier let three tills meet every evening, a semaphore kept the bank's limit of five, and a phaser let a helper go home early.

Now search your own code for countDown() and release(). Each countDown() belongs in a finally, and each release() must match an acquire() that really happened. An acquire() inside the try that releases it is a car park sign waiting to show six free spaces.

Every tool here exists because threads share something. Next, we'll take the sharing away: if nothing is shared, or nothing ever changes, what is left to protect?

sections.h: Waiting for three jobs to finish: the one-shot CountDownLatch
sections.html:
Let's write the naive version first, so we can watch it fail. The thread that opens the doors starts the three loads, naps for a fixed time and opens:

Java
// Naive: a guess about how long loading takes
startLoading();            // three threads: 200, 300 and 400 ms
Thread.sleep(250);
openDoors();
Kotlin
// Naive: a guess about how long loading takes
startLoading()             // three threads: 200, 300 and 400 ms
Thread.sleep(250)
openDoors()

The Try it below runs exactly this, with loads that take 200, 300 and 400 ms. It printed:

  220 ms  price list loaded
  271 ms  doors open after a 250 ms nap, lists still loading: 2

Two of the three lists were still loading when the first customer walked in. A longer nap would pass this run, and it would still be a guess, because loading time changes with the machine, the network and the day.

We don't want to wait for a time. We want to wait for three events: the prices are in, the stock counts are in, the offers are in. (The aside below explains why waiting for the threads to end with join() isn't the answer either.)

java.util.concurrent, the package of concurrency tools that comes with Java, has a class for exactly this job. A CountDownLatch is a gate with a counter on it. It starts at a count, here 3. Any thread can call countDown() to lower the count by one. Threads that call await() wait at the gate until the count reaches zero, and then all of them go through at once. You met a latch with a count of 1 in Race conditions: it was the starting gun that released all the test threads together.

Java
CountDownLatch loaded = new CountDownLatch(3);

// each loading thread, when its list is in (in a finally):
loaded.countDown();

// the thread that opens the doors:
if (!loaded.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("lists not loaded after 2 s");
}
openDoors();
Kotlin
val loaded = CountDownLatch(3)

// each loading thread, when its list is in (in a finally):
loaded.countDown()

// the thread that opens the doors:
if (!loaded.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    throw IllegalStateException("lists not loaded after 2 s")
}
openDoors()

Let's read it in order. First we make a latch with a count of 3, one for each list. Each loading thread calls countDown() when its list is in, inside a finally, so a load that fails still counts. Finally the door thread waits at the gate. Read its if aloud: wait until all three lists have loaded, but no longer than two seconds.

The same run with the latch printed:

  228 ms  price list loaded
  328 ms  today's offers loaded
  428 ms  stock counts loaded
  428 ms  ready=true, count=0

The doors opened the moment the slowest list arrived, no earlier and no later. Notice what the latch counted: events, not threads. One thread could count down three times, or three threads once each. The latch doesn't care who calls countDown(), only how many times.

One level down, the count is a single int inside the latch. countDown() lowers it with a compare-and-set, the "update it only if nobody beat me to it" call from Atomics and compare-and-set. The call that takes it to zero wakes every waiting thread, and no method ever raises it again. So a latch is one-shot: once it's open, it stays open. Every later await() returns at once, an extra countDown() does nothing, and there's no reset.

A latch also carries visibility. Everything a loading thread did before its countDown() happens-before await() returns in the door thread. Happens-before is the Java memory model's promise that one thread sees what another wrote, and the memory model track explains it. Here it means the door thread can read the three lists with no extra lock.

Two habits keep a latch from hanging a program. If a loading thread throws before it reaches countDown(), the count never gets to zero, and a plain await() waits forever. A thread dump, a printout of every thread's state and the method calls it is in the middle of, shows the door thread WAITING inside CountDownLatch.await. Nothing is left that could ever wake it.

A latch that misses one countDown() waits forever. Count down in finally, and await with a deadline.

The deadline is the second habit. await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) returns false if time runs out, so the program can say "the stock counts didn't load" instead of hanging in silence. The Try it makes one load hang for a minute so you can see it.

A latch opens once and stays open. That suits a morning. It doesn't suit a group that has to meet again every evening.

try.title: Open the shop when the lists are in
steps: Read LatchDemo. Three threads load three lists (200, 400 and 300 ms) and count down a latch. main opens the doors when the latch opens, waiting at most 2 seconds.
Run it with -Pargs=sleep first, the naive nap. Then predict when ready is printed in the latch version, and what an extra countDown() does after that.
Run it with no arguments. Then run it with -Pargs=stuck, where one load takes a minute.

code.title: LatchDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A shop's program loads three lists in parallel and opens its doors when all three are loaded. * Run with -Pargs=sleep to open after a fixed 250 ms nap instead, or -Pargs=stuck to make one load hang. */ public class LatchDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "latch"; String[] lists = {"price list", "stock counts", "today's offers"}; long[] loadMs = {200, 400, mode.equals("stuck") ? 60_000 : 300}; CountDownLatch loaded = new CountDownLatch(lists.length); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < lists.length; i++) { String name = lists[i]; long ms = loadMs[i]; Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(ms); // pretend to load System.out.printf("%5d ms %s loaded%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, name); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { loaded.countDown(); // count down even if loading failed } }, "load-" + i); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } if (mode.equals("sleep")) { // Naive: a guess about how long loading takes Thread.sleep(250); System.out.printf("%5d ms doors open after a 250 ms nap, lists still loading: %d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, loaded.getCount()); return; } boolean ready = loaded.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // never wait forever at startup System.out.printf("%5d ms ready=%s, count=%d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ready, loaded.getCount()); // a latch is one-shot: once at zero, await() returns at once, forever if (ready) { loaded.countDown(); System.out.println("after another countDown(): count=" + loaded.getCount() + ", await returns at once: " + loaded.await(0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); } } }

alt.title: LatchDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A shop's program loads three lists in parallel and opens its doors when all three are loaded. // Run with -Pargs=sleep to open after a fixed 250 ms nap instead, or -Pargs=stuck to make one load hang. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "latch" val lists = listOf("price list" to 200L, "stock counts" to 400L, "today's offers" to if (mode == "stuck") 60_000L else 300L) val loaded = CountDownLatch(lists.size) val t0 = System.nanoTime() for ((i, list) in lists.withIndex()) { val (name, ms) = list thread(isDaemon = true, name = "load-$i") { try { Thread.sleep(ms) // pretend to load println("%5d ms %s loaded".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, name)) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { loaded.countDown() // count down even if loading failed } } } if (mode == "sleep") { // Naive: a guess about how long loading takes Thread.sleep(250) println("%5d ms doors open after a 250 ms nap, lists still loading: %d" .format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, loaded.count)) return } val ready = loaded.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // never wait forever at startup println("%5d ms ready=%s, count=%d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ready, loaded.count)) // a latch is one-shot: once at zero, await() returns at once, forever if (ready) { loaded.countDown() println("after another countDown(): count=${loaded.count}, await returns at once: ${loaded.await(0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)}") } }

try.expect: With sleep, the doors open at about 250 ms with 2 lists still loading. With the latch, the lists arrive at about 200, 300 and 400 ms (plus a few ms to start up), and ready=true, count=0 follows right after the slowest one. The extra countDown() leaves the count at 0, and await returns at once. With stuck, main prints ready=false, count=1 after 2 seconds instead of hanging.

aside.title: Threads from zero waited with join(). Why not here?
aside.html: join() waits for a thread to end. Our loading threads happen to end when their list is in, so join() would work today. But a thread that keeps running after its first job never ends: say it loads the prices, then reloads them every hour. A join() on it waits forever. And once you hand tasks to a thread pool, a fixed group of threads that is reused for many tasks (the thread pools track), the thread outlives every task it runs. A latch waits for the event you care about, whoever makes it happen and whatever that thread does next.

video.title: Four ways to wait: a latch is a gate whose counter opens it once, a barrier is a tour bus that leaves when everyone is back, a phaser lets one go home, and a semaphore is a car park whose sign trusts every release

sections.h: Meeting at the end of every day: the CyclicBarrier
sections.html:
The shop's year of sales from Threads from zero comes back, with a twist. The shop has three tills, the cash registers at its counter, and three threads add them up, one till each, one day at a time. At the end of each day, someone adds the three subtotals into the day's total and sends the day's report. No thread may start the next day until that's done.

So the three threads have to meet at the end of every day. Let's try the tool we know first. Each thread counts down a latch of 3 when its till is done and then waits on it, and when the latch opens, thread 0 adds up the day. Day 1 works. Day 2 is worth tracing:

  1. Thread 0 finishes its till first, counts down and calls await(). The count is still zero from yesterday, so await() returns at once.
  2. Thread 0 adds up the day while threads 1 and 2 are still counting their tills, so the total uses yesterday's numbers for two tills.
  3. Thread 0 moves on to day 3, a day ahead of the others.

A one-shot gate can't close again behind the group. We'd need a fresh latch every day, and someone to hand it out at exactly the right moment, which is a new race.

What we want is a meeting point that resets itself, and that's a CyclicBarrier. You give it a number of parties, the threads that must meet, here 3. Each thread calls await() when it reaches the meeting point and waits there until the last party arrives. Then all of them go on together, and the barrier closes again for the next round. That reset is the cyclic part.

A tour bus works the same way. At every stop, the bus leaves only when everyone is back on board, and the guide counts heads before it moves off. The barrier is the bus, and the guide's head count is the barrier action. That's code the barrier runs once per round, on the last thread to arrive, before anyone is released.

Java
CyclicBarrier endOfDay = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> report(sum(sales)));   // the barrier action

// each of the 3 till threads, for every day:
sales[me] = addUp(me, day);
endOfDay.await();          // the 3rd to arrive runs the action, then all 3 go on
Kotlin
val endOfDay = CyclicBarrier(3) { report(sales.sum()) }   // the barrier action

// each of the 3 till threads, for every day:
sales[me] = addUp(me, day)
endOfDay.await()          // the 3rd to arrive runs the action, then all 3 go on

Each thread writes only its own slot of sales, before it calls await(). The barrier action then adds the three slots, and it can read them with no lock. Everything before await() happens-before the barrier action, and the action happens-before each thread's return from await(). The figure shows two days. The bars are work, the dashes are waiting, and the slowest till runs the action.

The Try it runs three tills for three days. It printed:

  day 1 closed by till-2: sales 6,000
  day 2 closed by till-2: sales 12,000
  day 3 closed by till-2: sales 18,000

Till 2 is the slowest, so it always arrives last and runs the action. One barrier served all three days.

Now the part that hurts in real programs: a barrier can break. If a waiting thread is interrupted (asked by another thread to stop), or its timed await runs out, or the barrier action throws, the barrier is broken. The thread that timed out gets TimeoutException, and every other waiting thread, now and later, gets BrokenBarrierException until someone calls reset(). That's on purpose. A round with a missing party can't finish, and failing everyone beats leaving them all waiting.

But look at what doesn't break it: a thread that throws before it ever reaches await(). A guide would go looking for a missing tourist. A barrier just waits, and with a plain await(), it waits forever. On day 4 of the Try it, till 2 never arrives, and the other two give up after 300 ms:

  till-0: TimeoutException, barrier now broken
  till-1: BrokenBarrierException

A barrier waits for every party, even one that will never come. Give await() a timeout.

In short, a latch is a gate opened by events ("three lists loaded"), once. A barrier is a meeting point for a fixed group of threads ("all three tills finished day 3"), every round.

Both of them make threads wait for each other. The next problem is the opposite one: too many threads doing the same thing at once.

try.title: Three days, then a missing till
steps: Read BarrierDemo. Three threads add up three tills for three days. The barrier action prints the day's sales and the name of the thread that ran it.
On day 4, till 2 never arrives, and the other two wait at most 300 ms. Predict what each of them prints.

code.title: BarrierDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException; import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** * Three threads add up the shop's three tills, day by day, and meet at one barrier that resets itself. * Then a day when one till never reports. */ public class BarrierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { long[] sales = new long[3]; // one slot per till, written by its own thread int[] day = {0}; CyclicBarrier endOfDay = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> // runs once per day, before anyone moves on System.out.printf(" day %d closed by %s: sales %,d%n", ++day[0], Thread.currentThread().getName(), sales[0] + sales[1] + sales[2])); Thread[] tills = new Thread[3]; for (int w = 0; w < 3; w++) { int me = w; tills[w] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int d = 1; d <= 3; d++) { Thread.sleep(50L * (me + 1)); // the tills finish at different times sales[me] = 1_000L * d * (me + 1); endOfDay.await(); // wait for the other two } // day 4: till 2 never reports, the others give up after 300 ms if (me == 2) return; endOfDay.await(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println(" " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": TimeoutException, barrier now broken"); } catch (BrokenBarrierException e) { System.out.println(" " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": BrokenBarrierException"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "till-" + w); tills[w].start(); } for (Thread t : tills) t.join(); System.out.println("broken: " + endOfDay.isBroken()); } }

alt.title: BarrierDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Three threads add up the shop's three tills, day by day, and meet at one barrier that resets itself. // Then a day when one till never reports. fun main() { val sales = LongArray(3) // one slot per till, written by its own thread var day = 0 val endOfDay = CyclicBarrier(3) { // runs once per day, before anyone moves on println(" day %d closed by %s: sales %,d".format(++day, Thread.currentThread().name, sales.sum())) } val tills = List(3) { me -> thread(name = "till-$me") { try { for (d in 1..3) { Thread.sleep(50L * (me + 1)) // the tills finish at different times sales[me] = 1_000L * d * (me + 1) endOfDay.await() // wait for the other two } // day 4: till 2 never reports, the others give up after 300 ms if (me != 2) endOfDay.await(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println(" ${Thread.currentThread().name}: TimeoutException, barrier now broken") } catch (e: BrokenBarrierException) { println(" ${Thread.currentThread().name}: BrokenBarrierException") } } } tills.forEach { it.join() } println("broken: ${endOfDay.isBroken}") }

try.expect: Three lines day N closed by till-2, with sales of 6,000, 12,000 and 18,000: till 2 is the slowest, so it always arrives last and runs the action. On day 4, one till gets TimeoutException and breaks the barrier, and the other gets BrokenBarrierException. Which one gets which can change between runs. broken: true at the end.

sections.h: Letting only five in at once: the Semaphore and its permits
sections.html:
The shop takes card payments, and a web service at the bank checks each one. A web service is a program on another computer that answers over the network. This one is the slow web service from Threads from zero: each call takes about 120 ms. The bank also has a rule. One shop may have at most five calls in progress at once, and it refuses a sixth.

On a busy Saturday, twenty customers pay at the same moment, so twenty threads call the bank together, and fifteen of them are refused. Fifteen customers are asked to try their card again. The shop needs to let five threads into the call at a time and make the others wait their turn.

A car park works this way. It has five spaces and a barrier at the entrance, with a sign that shows how many spaces are free. A car that drives in takes a space, and the sign counts down. A car that leaves gives one back, and the sign counts up. When the sign shows zero, the next car waits at the entrance until someone leaves.

A Semaphore is that car park in code. It holds a number of permits, here 5. acquire() takes a permit, and waits while none are left. release() gives one back. So at most five threads can be between the two calls at any moment:

Java
private final Semaphore bankPermits = new Semaphore(5);

Approval check(Payment p) throws InterruptedException {
    bankPermits.acquire();             // before the try, like lock()
    try {
        return bank.check(p);          // at most 5 threads in here
    } finally {
        bankPermits.release();
    }
}
Kotlin
private val bankPermits = Semaphore(5)

fun check(p: Payment): Approval {
    bankPermits.acquire()              // before the try, like lock()
    try {
        return bank.check(p)           // at most 5 threads in here
    } finally {
        bankPermits.release()
    }
}

The idiom is the one from Explicit locks: acquire() on the line before the try, release() in the finally. The Try it sends twenty calls through a Semaphore(5). Correctness first: the most calls in flight at once was 5. Then time: 502 ms, which is four waves of five calls at 120 ms each, plus a little start-up. tryAcquire(timeout, unit) waits a bounded time and returns false if no permit came free, so a payment can fail fast with a clear message instead of joining a long line.

Now the surprise from the warm-up. A lock, the key that lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, knows which thread holds it. It throws if a stranger tries to release it. A semaphore knows nothing of the kind. Permits have no owner. A semaphore is just a counter, and release() adds one, whoever calls it. The car park's sign believes every car that says it's leaving. The Try it ends by proving it:

new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): 6 permits

The sign now shows six free spaces in a car park built for five. That freedom is useful, since one thread can acquire a permit and another can release it. It's also how two common bugs quietly raise the limit:

  • calling acquire() inside the try, so a wait that is interrupted still runs the release() in finally (a waiting acquire() answers an interrupt by throwing InterruptedException);
  • ignoring what tryAcquire returns, then making the call and releasing anyway.

The lab's IssuerGate has both bugs. Each stray release is an extra permit for good. Over a day of cancelled payments and timeouts, a limit of 5 drifts to 8, then 12. The bank starts refusing calls again, and no exception or log line explains why.

A semaphore trusts every release. Release only the permits you took.

Two more details. A Semaphore limits one running program. If the shop runs three copies of its program on three computers, each with 5 permits, the bank sees up to 15 calls at once. Divide the bank's limit by the number of copies. And new Semaphore(5, true) makes it fair: waiting threads get permits in the order they arrived, so a fast thread can't keep grabbing a free permit ahead of one that has waited longer.

A latch, a barrier and a semaphore all have their number fixed the day you create them. The last tool is for a group that changes size.

try.title: Five permits, twenty calls
steps: Read SemaphoreDemo. Twenty threads each make a 120 ms call to the bank through a Semaphore(5), and the demo tracks the peak number of calls in flight.
Predict the peak and the total time. Then run it.
In the Java version, move bank.acquire() to just inside the inner try. Does anything change in this run? Why might it on a busy day?

code.title: SemaphoreDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 20 card checks, 5 permits, a slow web service that takes 120 ms per call. Then the bug that adds permits out of thin air. */ public class SemaphoreDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore bank = new Semaphore(5); // the bank's service allows 5 calls at once AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), peak = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] requests = new Thread[20]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < requests.length; i++) { requests[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { bank.acquire(); // before the try try { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(120); // the call to the slow web service inFlight.decrementAndGet(); } finally { bank.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); requests[i].start(); } for (Thread t : requests) t.join(); System.out.printf("20 calls, peak in flight %d, took %d ms%n", peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); // permits belong to nobody: any thread can release, even one that never acquired Semaphore carPark = new Semaphore(5); carPark.release(); System.out.println("new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): " + carPark.availablePermits() + " permits"); } }

alt.title: SemaphoreDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 20 card checks, 5 permits, a slow web service that takes 120 ms per call. Then the bug that adds permits out of thin air. private inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() // before the try try { return block() } finally { release() } } fun main() { val bank = Semaphore(5) // the bank's service allows 5 calls at once val inFlight = AtomicInteger() val peak = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val requests = List(20) { thread { bank.withPermit { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max) Thread.sleep(120) // the call to the slow web service inFlight.decrementAndGet() } } } requests.forEach { it.join() } println("20 calls, peak in flight ${peak.get()}, took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") // permits belong to nobody: any thread can release, even one that never acquired val carPark = Semaphore(5) carPark.release() println("new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): ${carPark.availablePermits()} permits") }

try.expect: Peak in flight 5, total about half a second (502 and 519 ms in runs here): four waves of five calls. The stray release() turns 5 permits into 6. Moving acquire() inside the try changes nothing in this run, because nobody interrupts the waiting threads. On a busy day an interrupt during the wait (a cancelled payment, a shutdown) would release a permit that was never taken.

sections.h: A group that changes size: the Phaser, and what all four can't do
sections.html:
Once a year, the shop counts its stock. The job runs in three phases: count every shelf, check the counts against the books, write the report. Three helpers start the job, and nobody may start checking before every shelf is counted. A barrier fits so far. Then it turns out that one helper was only booked for the counting, and goes home when it's done.

With a CyclicBarrier(3), the two helpers who stay would wait at the end of the check phase for a third party who has gone home. They'd wait forever, or until a timeout broke the barrier. A barrier's number of parties is fixed when you create it.

A Phaser is a barrier whose group can change size. A thread calls register() to join. It calls arriveAndAwaitAdvance() at the end of a phase, which waits just like await() on a barrier. And it calls arriveAndDeregister() to arrive one last time and leave. Each phase waits only for the parties registered at that moment. Phases are numbered from 0, and you can override onAdvance(phase, parties) to run code between phases, which makes it the phaser's barrier action. When onAdvance returns true, the phaser ends.

Java
Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1);          // the main thread is a party until it leaves
phaser.register();                      // each helper joins before it starts
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();         // end of a phase: wait for everyone still registered
phaser.arriveAndDeregister();           // arrive one last time and leave
Kotlin
val phaser = Phaser(1)          // the main thread is a party until it leaves
phaser.register()               // each helper joins before it starts
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance()  // end of a phase: wait for everyone still registered
phaser.arriveAndDeregister()    // arrive one last time and leave

The Try it runs the stocktake, and its onAdvance prints each phase with the parties still taking part:

  phase 0 (count) done, 3 parties
  phase 1 (check) done, 2 parties
  phase 2 (report) done, 2 parties
terminated: true

Helper 2 counted with the others. At the check phase, its arriveAndDeregister() arrived and left in one call, so that phase didn't wait for it, and no later phase counted it. Notice the 1 in new Phaser(1): the main thread registers itself first, so no phase can finish while helpers are still joining, and it leaves once all three have joined. Use a phaser when the number of workers isn't known up front or changes between phases. When the group is fixed, a CyclicBarrier is simpler and says what it means.

The smallest synchronizer needs only two sentences. An Exchanger lets exactly two threads meet and swap one object each, for example a full basket for an empty one. You'll rarely need it.

Now the limits, which all of these tools share. Each one parks its waiting threads, that is, puts them to sleep until something wakes them. In a thread dump they show as WAITING or TIMED_WAITING, with the tool's class in the stack. And none of them has an owner. That's what makes them flexible, and it's also why the deadlock detector from Deadlock, livelock and starvation, built into the JVM (the program that runs your Java code), can't see through them. (A deadlock is a group of threads that wait for each other forever.) Twenty threads that each hold one permit and wait for a second are deadlocked, and the dump reports nothing. You find them by reading the stacks.

In real programs you'll often get these tools without creating them yourself. The thread pools track shows invokeAll and CompletableFuture.allOf, which each do a latch's job in one call. They're built from the same parts, so when one of them hangs, the thread dump shows the same parked threads.

try.title: A helper goes home early
steps: Read PhaserDemo. Three helpers run three phases (count, check, report). Helper 2 leaves after the counting. onAdvance prints each phase and the parties left.
Predict the party count printed for each phase.
Run it. Then explain what would happen with a CyclicBarrier(3) instead.

code.title: PhaserDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.Phaser; /** A stocktake in three phases. Helper 2 only counts, then goes home; the Phaser just has fewer parties. */ public class PhaserDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String[] phases = {"count", "check", "report"}; Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1) { // 1 party: main, until it deregisters @Override protected boolean onAdvance(int phase, int parties) { System.out.printf(" phase %d (%s) done, %d parties%n", phase, phases[phase], parties); return phase == phases.length - 1 || parties == 0; // true ends the phaser } }; Thread[] helpers = new Thread[3]; for (int w = 0; w < helpers.length; w++) { int me = w; phaser.register(); // a new party joins helpers[w] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < phases.length; p++) { if (me == 2 && p == 1) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // helper 2 only counts, then leaves return; } phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); // like a barrier, for this phase } }, "helper-" + w); helpers[w].start(); } phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // main stops taking part for (Thread t : helpers) t.join(); System.out.println("terminated: " + phaser.isTerminated()); } }

alt.title: PhaserDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.Phaser import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A stocktake in three phases. Helper 2 only counts, then goes home; the Phaser just has fewer parties. fun main() { val phases = listOf("count", "check", "report") val phaser = object : Phaser(1) { // 1 party: main, until it deregisters override fun onAdvance(phase: Int, parties: Int): Boolean { println(" phase %d (%s) done, %d parties".format(phase, phases[phase], parties)) return phase == phases.lastIndex || parties == 0 // true ends the phaser } } val helpers = List(3) { me -> phaser.register() // a new party joins thread(name = "helper-$me") { for (p in phases.indices) { if (me == 2 && p == 1) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // helper 2 only counts, then leaves return@thread } phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance() // like a barrier, for this phase } } } phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // main stops taking part helpers.forEach { it.join() } println("terminated: ${phaser.isTerminated}") }

try.expect: phase 0 (count) done, 3 parties, then phase 1 (check) done, 2 parties and phase 2 (report) done, 2 parties, then terminated: true. main registered itself first so no phase could finish before every helper had joined, then left. With a CyclicBarrier(3), the two helpers who stay would wait at the end of the check phase for helper 2, who has gone home.

compare.title: A permit helper in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Java
java.html: static <T> T withPermit(Semaphore s, Callable<T> task) throws Exception { s.acquire(); // before the try, like lock() try { return task.call(); } finally { s.release(); // exactly the permit we took } } Approval a = withPermit(bankPermits, () -> bank.check(payment));

kotlin.title: Kotlin
kotlin.html: inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() // before the try, like lock() try { return block() } finally { release() // exactly the permit we took } } val a = bankPermits.withPermit { bank.check(payment) }

compare.note: Both versions use the same java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, and both block a thread while it waits for a permit. Java does the job well with a static helper that takes a Callable, and every caller passes a lambda. Kotlin's version is an extension function, one you call as if it were a method of Semaphore itself. It is also inline, so the compiler copies the lambda's code into each call site: no object is created, and a return inside the block works as usual. The safe idiom then reads like part of the language, and nobody writes the try and finally by hand again. The Kotlin standard library doesn't ship withPermit for this Semaphore, so you write it once, as here. kotlinx.coroutines has a Semaphore of its own with a built-in withPermit, which suspends a coroutine instead of blocking a thread; the coroutines track covers it.

worked.title: Adding up four tills without hanging

steps.say: At closing time, the shop adds up its four tills. Each till takes a few seconds, so four threads do the work, and the main thread waits for all of them with a latch. Read this first version. What happens if addUp throws for one till, say because a receipt can't be read?
steps.code: // Naive: one bad receipt and this never ends CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(4); List<Long> totals = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); for (Till till : tills) { new Thread(() -> { totals.add(addUp(till)); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); report(totals);

alt.html: // Naive: one bad receipt and this never ends val done = CountDownLatch(4) val totals = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Long>() for (till in tills) { thread { totals.add(addUp(till)) done.countDown() } } done.await() report(totals)

steps.say: The failing thread dies before it reaches countDown(). The count stays at 1, and await() waits forever. The program doesn't fail; it just never finishes. A thread dump shows main WAITING in CountDownLatch.await, and no till threads at all, because they have all finished or died. The fix has three parts: count down in finally, keep the failure so it isn't lost, and never wait without a deadline.
Here's the version that always ends, with a label on each step.
steps.code: CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tills.size()); List<Long> totals = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<Throwable> failures = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); for (Till till : tills) { new Thread(() -> { try { totals.add(addUp(till)); // 1. do the work } catch (Throwable e) { failures.add(e); // 2. keep the failure instead of losing it } finally { done.countDown(); // 3. always count down } }, "till-" + till.id()).start(); } if (!done.await(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 4. never wait forever throw new IllegalStateException("tills still adding up after 1 min"); } if (!failures.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("tills failed: " + failures); report(totals); // 5. countDown happens-before await returns: all totals visible

alt.html: val done = CountDownLatch(tills.size) val totals = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Long>() val failures = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Throwable>() for (till in tills) { thread(name = "till-${till.id}") { try { totals.add(addUp(till)) // 1. do the work } catch (e: Throwable) { failures.add(e) // 2. keep the failure instead of losing it } finally { done.countDown() // 3. always count down } } } if (!done.await(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 4. never wait forever throw IllegalStateException("tills still adding up after 1 min") } if (failures.isNotEmpty()) throw IllegalStateException("tills failed: $failures") report(totals) // 5. countDown happens-before await returns: all totals visible

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself why main can read totals after await returns, without any lock. Answer: everything a till thread did before its countDown() happens-before await() returns in the waiting thread. totals is still a CopyOnWriteArrayList, a thread-safe list from Concurrent collections, because four threads add to it at the same time. In a real program you'd hand the four jobs to a thread pool and wait for all of them with invokeAll, which the thread pools track covers. A latch is one of the parts such tools are built from.

lab.title: Fix a permit leak, then add up sales in rounds
steps: Meet the two classes. IssuerGate is the shop's gate in front of the bank's card service from the third section (the bank behind a card is called its issuer). It lets at most maxConcurrent calls run at once, and it has both permit bugs. RoundRunner runs a job in rounds on several threads: in each round every worker computes its share, and the round's total is passed on once, just as the tills did for each day.
Run the tests. Four of the six fail: the timed call runs its task with no permit, a caller interrupted while it waits adds a permit, and both RoundRunner tests hit UnsupportedOperationException.
Fix IssuerGate.call(task): move acquire() to the line before the try.
Fix IssuerGate.call(task, maxWait): if tryAcquire returns false, throw TimeoutException before the try, so the task doesn't run and nothing is released.

Write RoundRunner.run. Keep a long[] shares, one slot per worker. Build a CyclicBarrier(workers, action) whose action sums shares and calls onRoundTotal. Start one thread per worker that loops over the rounds: shares[me] = step.applyAsLong(me, r), then await(). Join every thread before returning.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: Why can the barrier action read shares without a lock? Each worker writes only its own slot, before await(), and everything before await() happens-before the action runs.
await() throws InterruptedException and BrokenBarrierException. In the worker, restore the interrupt flag for the first, and stop the loop for both.

The second RoundRunner test calls your step from 4 threads and checks that round r never starts before r totals have been passed on. The barrier action runs before anyone is released, so this holds by construction.
lab.done: All six tests in SynchronizersTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Wait for N tasks, with a deadline
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write awaitAll(tasks, deadline): run each task on its own thread and return true if all of them finished within the deadline, false otherwise. A task that throws must not make it hang. Then check: where is your countDown()?

answer.html: static boolean awaitAll(List<Runnable> tasks, Duration deadline) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks.size()); for (Runnable task : tasks) { new Thread(() -> { try { task.run(); } finally { done.countDown(); // even when the task throws } }).start(); } return done.await(deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: fun awaitAll(tasks: List<() -> Unit>, deadline: Duration): Boolean { val done = CountDownLatch(tasks.size) for (task in tasks) { thread { try { task() } finally { done.countDown() // even when the task throws } } } return done.await(deadline.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) }

recap: CountDownLatch waits until N events have happened, once. Count down in finally, await with a timeout, and everything written before countDown() is visible after await().
CyclicBarrier makes N threads meet every round. The barrier action runs once, on the last to arrive, then all go on, and the barrier resets itself.
A barrier breaks on a timeout or an interrupt, but a thread that never reaches await() leaves the others waiting forever unless they use the timed await.
Semaphore lets at most N threads in at once. Permits have no owner, so release only what you took: acquire() before try, and check what tryAcquire returns.
Phaser is a barrier whose parties can join and leave between phases. Exchanger swaps one object between two threads.
The limit: none of these tools has an owner, so a missing countDown() or a stray release() fails silently, and the deadlock detector can't see a cycle through them.

explain.prompt: Explain the difference between a CountDownLatch, a CyclicBarrier and a Semaphore to a friend who is new to threads, with one everyday example of each.
explain.answer: A latch waits for a number of events and then opens for good: the shop's door thread waits until the price list, the stock counts and the offers have loaded, then opens. A barrier is a meeting point for a fixed group of threads, every round, like a tour bus that leaves each stop only when everyone is back on board. Three till threads each finish day 3, the last one to arrive adds up the day, and then all three start day 4. A semaphore limits how many threads do something at the same time, like a car park with five spaces: at most five threads may be inside a call to the bank. The traps differ too. A latch hangs if a task forgets to count down. A barrier hangs if a thread never arrives and nobody gave await a timeout. A semaphore quietly raises its limit if code releases a permit it never took.

deeper.html:
CountDownLatch and Semaphore, like ReentrantLock, are thin layers over AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, a JDK class that holds one int of state and a queue of parked threads. For a latch the state is the count, and await parks until it is zero. For a semaphore it is the number of permits left. CyclicBarrier is a ReentrantLock with one Condition, and Phaser and Exchanger keep their own queues of parked threads. All of them park through LockSupport, which is why they look the same in a thread dump: WAITING (parking), with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore$NonfairSync).

A few corners of the API are worth knowing. Semaphore.acquire(n) takes several permits in one step, which avoids the hold-one-and-wait-for-another deadlock from the quiz. drainPermits() takes all that are left, which is handy when you want to stop new work during a shutdown. acquireUninterruptibly() ignores interrupts, which you almost never want. CyclicBarrier.await() returns the arrival index (parties minus one for the first to arrive, zero for the last), so you can pick one thread to do extra work without a barrier action.

Phaser supports tiering: you can build a tree of phasers so that thousands of parties don't all compete for one. Its Javadoc caps a single phaser at 65,535 registered parties.

Virtual threads (JDK 21) are very light threads that the JVM runs on a few ordinary ones. Blocking in any of these tools is cheap there: the virtual thread parks, and the ordinary thread under it runs something else. A Semaphore is in fact the standard way to limit how many calls run at once when you start a virtual thread per task, because there's no pool size to do it for you. The virtual threads track comes back to that. In Kotlin coroutines, the equivalents suspend instead of blocking: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore, Job.join() or awaitAll() where you'd use a latch, and channels for most of the rest.
